title: Kafka internals
scopeHtml: Scope: partitions, replication, ISR, offsets, retention, compaction and sizing.

notes.title: The broker, partition and segment layout
notes.html:
A Kafka partition is a directory of segment files on a broker's disk; messages are appended sequentially. Each message gets an increasing offset within its partition. A segment (default log.segment.bytes = 1 GiB) is rolled when full or after log.roll.hours; old segments are deleted or compacted as whole files.

Why Kafka is fast: sequential disk writes, the OS page cache (the broker leans on it rather than its own heap cache), batching and compression, and zero-copy sendfile from page cache to the network socket. A modest broker can sustain hundreds of MB/s.

topic orders, partition 0
00000000000000000000.log   offsets 0..99,999
00000000000000100000.log   offsets 100,000..  (active segment)
each segment also has .index (offset->position) and .timeindex

Worked example. A topic gets 50 MB/s in. At 1 GiB segments, a new segment rolls about every 20 s. Reading a recent offset is served from RAM; reading data from 3 days ago hits disk and can evict hot pages for others (a known cause of latency spikes when a consumer replays history).

Industry examples. LinkedIn originally designed this layout; Kafka powers Uber, Netflix and most data platforms with the same storage design.

Everyday analogy. A notebook where each page is numbered; you only ever write at the end and bookmark where you stopped reading.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Kafka is fast because it is "in memory". It is disk-based, sequential, and relies on page cache.
  • Using a huge number of tiny partitions; each costs file handles and metadata.

notes.title: Replication, leader and ISR
notes.html:
Each partition has one leader and N-1 follower replicas on other brokers. Producers and consumers talk to the leader; followers copy from it. The ISR (in-sync replicas) is the set of replicas caught up with the leader (within replica.lag.time.max.ms, default 30 s in recent versions; confirm for your version).

Key settings:

  • replication.factor=3
  • min.insync.replicas=2
  • Producer acks=all (or -1): the leader waits for all ISR members to have the write.

With RF=3, min.insync=2, acks=all: you survive 1 broker loss without data loss and without losing availability for writes. If the ISR shrinks to 1, writes are rejected (NotEnoughReplicas) rather than accepting data that is not safely stored. unclean.leader.election.enable=false (the default) prevents an out-of-sync replica from becoming leader, trading availability for no data loss.

acks Meaning Risk
0 Fire and forget Lost on any failure
1 Leader wrote it Lost if leader dies before followers copy
all All ISR wrote it Safe up to min.insync loss

Gravity. The replication factor cannot easily be changed without reassigning partitions; choose 3 up front for important topics (a costly-to-reverse, but doable, operation). Cross-AZ placement (broker.rack) lets you survive a zone loss.

Industry examples. Banks and payment companies run RF=3, min.insync=2, acks=all. Metrics: UnderReplicatedPartitions greater than 0 is the classic alarm.

Everyday analogy. Writing the meeting minutes and getting two colleagues to confirm their copies before declaring "saved".

Common interview traps.

  • acks=all with min.insync.replicas=1 gives no extra safety once the ISR drops to the leader alone.
  • Enabling unclean election for availability and silently losing committed messages.

notes.title: Offsets and commits
notes.html:
An offset is a consumer's bookmark per partition. Committed offsets are stored in the internal topic __consumer_offsets, per (group, topic, partition). The committed value is the next offset to read.

  • Auto-commit (enable.auto.commit=true, every 5 s by default): easy, but it can commit before processing finishes (loss on crash) or after (duplicates).
  • Manual commit after processing: at-least-once. Commit before processing: at-most-once.
  • auto.offset.reset=earliest|latest decides where a brand-new group starts.
  • Lag = latest offset minus committed offset; the key health metric.
while (true) {
  var records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500));
  for (var r : records) handle(r);       // must be idempotent
  consumer.commitSync();                 // commit after processing
}

Worked example. Handler takes 40 ms per record, poll returns 500 records: 20 s of work. If max.poll.interval.ms is 300 s you are fine; if it is 10 s the consumer is kicked from the group, a rebalance happens and the batch is processed again by someone else. Lower max.poll.records or speed up the handler.

Industry examples. Every Kafka consumer app (Spring Kafka, Kafka Streams). Tools: kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group billing shows lag per partition.

Everyday analogy. A bookmark: move it only after you actually finished the page.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a commit means "processed" rather than "I promise I will start here".
  • Long processing causing rebalance storms from max.poll.interval.ms.

notes.title: Retention and log compaction
notes.html:
Kafka deletes by time or size, or keeps only the latest value per key (compaction).

  • Delete policy: retention.ms (default 7 days), retention.bytes. Deletion works on whole segments, so data may live a little longer than the limit.
  • Compact policy (cleanup.policy=compact): for each key, keep at least the latest record; older ones are removed in the background. A tombstone (key with null value) marks a deletion and is itself removed after delete.retention.ms. The newest active segment is not compacted.
  • Both: cleanup.policy=compact,delete.
Before compaction:  k1=a, k2=b, k1=c, k3=d, k2=null
After compaction:   k1=c, k3=d          (k2 tombstoned then removed)

Use cases. Compaction suits changelogs and state: a "user profile" topic, KTable backing topics in Kafka Streams, __consumer_offsets itself, CDC from a database (rebuild current state from the topic). Delete retention suits event streams (clicks, logs).

Worked example. Config topic with 10M updates for 200k keys: after compaction roughly 200k records remain, so a new consumer bootstraps in seconds rather than replaying 10M.

Industry examples. Debezium CDC topics, Kafka Streams state stores, Schema Registry's _schemas topic.

Everyday analogy. A contacts list: you keep only the latest phone number per person, not every number they ever had.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting compaction to be immediate or to remove all old values instantly.
  • Keys must not be null in compacted topics.
  • Treating tombstones as instant deletes (consumers must still see them for the retention window).

notes.title: Sizing a Kafka cluster
notes.html:
Size by throughput, retention and consumer parallelism. Work through the numbers.

Worked example. 20,000 msgs/s at 1 KB = 20 MB/s ingest. Retention 7 days, RF=3.

  • Daily data: 20 MB/s x 86,400 = about 1.73 TB. Seven days = about 12.1 TB.
  • With RF=3: about 36.3 TB raw. Add 30% headroom: about 47 TB. On brokers with 8 TB usable each, about 6 brokers.
  • Network: ingest 20 MB/s, replication adds 2 x 20 = 40 MB/s out of leaders to followers, consumers (say 3 groups) read 60 MB/s. About 120 MB/s per cluster, split over 6 brokers: easy for 10 GbE.
  • Partitions: target throughput per partition is about 5 to 10 MB/s write for one partition (varies, benchmark). For 20 MB/s, 6 partitions suffice for ingest; but if each consumer handles 2,000 msgs/s, you need 10 consumers, so choose 12 to 24 partitions for headroom and parallelism. A rough guide is a few thousand partitions per broker as a ceiling (newer KRaft versions handle many more; confirm for your version).

Config levers: compression (lz4 or zstd, 2 to 4x smaller for JSON), linger.ms=5-20 with batch.size=64KB for throughput.

Gravity. Partition count is easy to increase and effectively impossible to decrease; start moderately (for example 12), grow later. Over-partitioning increases rebalance time and recovery.

Industry examples. LinkedIn reported trillions of messages/day; Uber and Netflix run multi-cluster setups with MirrorMaker or Replicator for cross-region.

Everyday analogy. Planning warehouse shelves: how fast boxes arrive, how long you keep them, and how many copies you store.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the RF multiplier on disk and network.
  • Choosing partitions from broker count rather than consumer parallelism and per-partition throughput.
  • Ignoring that ZooKeeper has been replaced by KRaft in modern Kafka (ZooKeeper removed in 4.0).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Partition = ordered segmented log on disk; speed comes from sequential I/O, page cache, batching, zero-copy.
  • RF=3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all, no unclean election for safe durability.
  • Offsets are consumer bookmarks in __consumer_offsets; commit after processing gives at-least-once.
  • Retention deletes whole segments by time/size; compaction keeps the latest value per key, with tombstones for deletes.
  • Size from MB/s x retention x RF; choose partitions from consumer parallelism; partitions can grow, not shrink.

questions.promptHtml: Kafka stores everything on disk, yet it does hundreds of MB/s. Why is it fast, and what exactly is a partition on the broker?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who say "it is in memory" from people who know the storage design.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A partition is a directory of append-only segment files; each message gets an increasing offset. It is fast because writes are sequential, the broker leans on the OS page cache instead of its own heap, messages are batched and compressed, and reads use zero-copy sendfile from page cache to the socket. Old data is removed by deleting whole segment files.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Sequential disk I/O is orders of magnitude faster than random I/O, and even spinning disks do it well. The broker never updates in place: it appends to the active segment (default log.segment.bytes = 1 GiB, or log.roll.hours). Each segment has a .index (offset to file position, sparse) and .timeindex. A consumer reading a recent offset is served from RAM (page cache); the kernel copies page cache straight to the NIC with sendfile, skipping user space.

topic orders, partition 0
00000000000000000000.log   offsets 0..99,999
00000000000000100000.log   offsets 100,000..  (active)
+ .index (offset->position), .timeindex

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Kafka is fast because it is in memory." It is disk-based; page cache does the caching.
  • Creating thousands of tiny partitions: each costs file handles and metadata.
  • Forgetting that a lagging consumer reading old data bypasses the cache.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why delete whole segments rather than single messages? -> Append-only files cannot be edited cheaply; dropping a file is O(1) and keeps writes sequential.
  2. How does a broker find offset 150,000? -> Binary search segment file names, then the sparse .index, then scan a few KB.
  3. What does a replay of 3-day-old data do to other consumers? -> Cold reads evict hot pages from the cache, raising latency for tail readers.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer lists "sequential I/O". The senior adds page cache dependence, zero-copy, sparse indexes, and the cache-eviction side effect of historical replays.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A backfill job replaying a week of data once raised p99 produce latency for a whole cluster because it flushed the page cache.

questions.promptHtml: Explain leader, followers and ISR. What do acks, min.insync.replicas and unclean.leader.election.enable do together, and what is the safe setup for payments?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Durability questions are the heart of Kafka interviews; most candidates only know acks=all.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each partition has one leader that serves reads and writes; followers copy from it. The ISR is the set of replicas that are caught up. With RF=3, min.insync.replicas=2, producer acks=all and unclean election off, a write is confirmed only when at least 2 replicas have it, so I survive one broker loss with no data loss and still accept writes. If the ISR drops to 1, writes are rejected rather than stored unsafely.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
acks=all waits for every replica currently in the ISR, not for all replicas. So if the ISR shrinks to just the leader, acks=all degenerates to acks=1 unless min.insync.replicas forces a floor (it makes the broker return NotEnoughReplicas). unclean.leader.election.enable=false means only an ISR member can become leader, so a stale replica never wins and silently discards committed messages; the cost is that the partition is unavailable if all ISR members are gone.

acks Meaning Risk
0 Fire and forget Lost on any failure
1 Leader wrote Lost if leader dies before followers copy
all All ISR wrote Safe up to min.insync loss

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# topic / producer settings
replication.factor: 3
min.insync.replicas: 2
acks: all
enable.idempotence: true
unclean.leader.election.enable: false

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• acks=all with min.insync.replicas=1: no extra safety once the ISR is one.
  • Enabling unclean election "for availability" and losing committed data.
  • All three replicas in one AZ; use broker.rack.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if 2 of 3 brokers die? -> ISR below 2, producers get NotEnoughReplicas; consistent but unavailable for writes.
  2. What puts a follower out of ISR? -> Lagging beyond replica.lag.time.max.ms (verify default for your version).
  3. When would you accept unclean election? -> Metrics/log topics where availability beats loss, as a deliberate per-topic choice.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use acks=all". Senior: the trio of settings, the ISR degeneration trap, rack awareness, and the CP-vs-AP trade being made explicitly.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team had min.insync.replicas=1; one broker restart during a deploy lost a few seconds of acknowledged orders.

questions.contextHtml:
A billing consumer uses defaults (enable.auto.commit=true, 5 s interval). After a pod OOM-kill during a deploy, finance says 212 invoices were never generated, yet consumer lag is 0.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
while (true) {
  var records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500));
  for (var r : records) executor.submit(() -> generateInvoice(r.value())); // async
}
while (true) {
  val records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500))
  for (r in records) executor.submit { generateInvoice(r.value()) } // async
}

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the commit interval" or "add retries". It misses that the commit is decoupled from processing completion.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is generateInvoice idempotent? How big is the executor queue? Did the crash coincide with a poll? These decide whether I can switch to at-least-once.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reset the group offset to a timestamp before the deploy (kafka-consumer-groups.sh --reset-offsets --to-datetime) and replay; invoices need a dedup key first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) auto-commit committed offsets for records still in the executor queue; (b) exceptions swallowed in the executor; (c) rebalance. Lag 0 matches (a).
  4. How I'd verify: Compare committed offsets with the generated-invoice order IDs; check the executor queue depth metric; look for lost futures.
  5. Root cause: Auto-commit commits on the next poll() whatever was returned, not what was processed. Async hand-off means "committed" is not "done"; a crash drops the queued work, which Kafka will never redeliver.
  6. Fix: Short term: process synchronously and commitSync() after the batch. Long term: manual commit after the async work finishes (track completed offsets per partition), idempotent invoice creation keyed by order ID.
  7. Prevention: Alert on lag plus an end-to-end reconciliation job; lint rule against auto-commit in critical consumers.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just lower the commit interval; it narrows, never closes, the window.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is lag 0 but data missing? -> Lag measures commits, not processing.
  • Can this produce duplicates too? -> Yes if processing finishes after a crash but before the next commit; hence idempotency.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: an "async for throughput" refactor silently turned at-least-once into at-most-once; it was found only by a monthly reconciliation.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks the interval.
  • Hire: identifies commit-before-process and proposes manual commits.
  • Strong hire: adds per-partition completed-offset tracking, idempotency and a reconciliation safety net.

questions.contextHtml: A new ride-events pipeline: 30,000 msgs/s at 800 bytes, retention 3 days, RF=3, 4 consumer groups (one is a 3 ms/msg enricher). Brokers have 6 TB usable disk and 10 GbE. Product wants 30% headroom.
questions.promptHtml: How many brokers and partitions? Show the math.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "3 brokers, 10 partitions" with no arithmetic, or forgetting the RF multiplier.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is 30k the peak or the average? Compression expected? Does any group need to replay beyond 3 days? Cross-AZ?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; I size first and state assumptions.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Disk binds first; network second; partition count is driven by consumer parallelism.
  4. How I'd verify: Compute, then benchmark with kafka-producer-perf-test.sh.
  5. Root cause (the numbers): Ingest = 30,000 x 800 B = 24 MB/s. Per day 24 MB/s x 86,400 = about 2.07 TB; 3 days about 6.2 TB; RF=3 about 18.7 TB; plus 30% headroom about 24.3 TB. At 6 TB per broker that is 4.05, so 5 brokers (6 for failure tolerance and rebalancing room). Network: 24 MB/s in, 48 MB/s replication, 4 groups x 24 = 96 MB/s out, about 170 MB/s total, trivial for 10 GbE across 5-6 brokers. Partitions: enricher at 3 ms/msg handles about 333 msg/s per thread, so 30,000 / 333 = 90 consumers; choose 96 partitions, not 12. Check that the per-partition rate of 24 MB/s / 96 = 0.25 MB/s is tiny, fine.
  6. Fix / recommendation: 6 brokers, 96 partitions, lz4/zstd (2-4x smaller, so disk may halve), linger.ms=10. Consider making the enricher async/batched to need fewer partitions.
  7. Prevention: Alert on disk above 70%, on under-replicated partitions and on consumer lag in seconds.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Partition count can grow but never shrink, so I would not pick 500 "just in case"; more partitions add rebalance time and file handles.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Retention becomes 14 days? -> Disk 4.7x: about 114 TB raw with headroom; consider tiered storage (verify availability in your version).
  • Traffic 10x? -> Network and partition count rise; benchmark; add brokers and reassign.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a cluster sized from ingest alone ran out of disk in week two because RF and a replay group's retention extension were ignored.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no math or no RF.
  • Hire: disk, network and partitions computed with RF and headroom.
  • Strong hire: partitions from consumer throughput, compression lever, failure headroom and benchmarking plan.

questions.promptHtml: When would you choose cleanup.policy=compact over delete retention, and how do tombstones work?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know Kafka can act as a state store, not just a queue.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Delete policy removes old segments by age or size, right for event streams like clicks. Compaction keeps at least the latest record per key, right for changelogs and state such as user profiles or CDC. A tombstone is a key with a null value that marks deletion; it is itself removed after delete.retention.ms.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The compactor works on closed segments, never the active one, so old values linger for a while. After compaction consumers still see every record in the uncompacted head, and only the latest per key in the cleaned tail. Both policies can be combined as compact,delete. Keys must be non-null. A new consumer bootstraps current state by reading the compacted topic: 10M updates for 200k keys leave about 200k records.

Before: k1=a, k2=b, k1=c, k3=d, k2=null
After:  k1=c, k3=d      (k2 tombstone later removed)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting immediate compaction.
  • Null keys in a compacted topic.
  • Expecting a tombstone to hide the key from consumers right away; it lives for the delete.retention.ms window so slow consumers see it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does compaction guarantee one record per key? -> No, only at least the latest; duplicates remain in the head.
  2. How do you GDPR-delete a user from a delete-retention topic? -> You cannot per key; use compaction with tombstones or crypto-shredding.
  3. Why is __consumer_offsets compacted? -> Only the latest committed offset per (group, topic, partition) matters.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "compaction keeps latest". Senior covers the active segment, tombstone lifecycle, lag in cleaning, and the privacy implications.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team assumed deletes were instant; a consumer lagging beyond delete.retention.ms never saw the tombstone and kept a deleted user in its cache.

questions.contextHtml:
An image-resize consumer group (8 consumers, 16 partitions) shows constant rebalancing. Logs:

WARN  Member consumer-7 sending LeaveGroup because consumer poll timeout has expired (max.poll.interval.ms=10000)
INFO  Revoking previously assigned partitions [resize-3]
INFO  (Re-)joining group
ERROR CommitFailedException: group has already rebalanced

max.poll.records is 500 (default). Each image takes ~80 ms. Lag keeps growing despite CPU being only 30%. Brokers look healthy.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the brokers or adds consumers, which worsens rebalances.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did anything change recently (image size, traffic, a deploy)? Is the timeout set deliberately? Is processing synchronous in the poll thread?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise max.poll.interval.ms to 300000 or drop max.poll.records to 50 and restart.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) 500 x 80 ms = 40 s of work per poll exceeds the 10 s limit; (b) GC pauses; (c) network. Math fits (a).
  4. How I'd verify: Time the loop per batch; kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group resize; rebalance-rate metric.
  5. Root cause: The member does not call poll() within the interval, is evicted, the batch is reassigned and reprocessed, so work is repeated and never commits: a rebalance storm with duplicate work.
  6. Fix: Short term: max.poll.records=50 (4 s per batch). Long term: process in worker threads with pause()/resume(), make resize idempotent, use static membership (group.instance.id) and cooperative rebalancing.
  7. Prevention: Alert on rebalance count and commit-failed rate; budget records x p99 time < 50% of interval.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just increase the interval to huge values; failure detection of a truly hung consumer slows down.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did CPU stay low? -> Work repeated and rebalance pauses idle the group.
  • Does a longer session.timeout.ms help? -> No; heartbeats are separate from poll interval.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a payload size increase doubled per-record time and tipped a group over the limit at 2 am; the storm only ended when batch size was halved.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames brokers.
  • Hire: connects the settings with the arithmetic.
  • Strong hire: adds pause/resume, static membership and the duplicate-work implication.

questions.contextHtml:
A payments topic (RF=3, min.insync.replicas=2, producers acks=all) at 12k msgs/s. At 14:02 producers log NotEnoughReplicasException; checkout error rate hits 40%. Metrics:

UnderReplicatedPartitions: 0 -> 118
ISR size (payments-*): 3 -> 1 on 118 partitions
broker-2: disk await 450 ms, CPU 20%
broker-3: network OK, GC pause 9 s at 14:01

A teammate proposes setting min.insync.replicas=1 right now.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do, and what is going on?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Agrees to set min.insync=1 to "restore service", ignoring data-loss risk.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it all partitions or those led by one broker? Did a deploy or disk event precede it? What is the business tolerance: unavailable checkout or possible lost payment events?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Do not lower min.insync blindly. If followers are slow, fix them: restart the GC-stalled broker-3, move traffic off broker-2 (shift leaders with preferred election). Producers can buffer and retry while we recover; consider a client-side fallback queue.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Followers fell behind past replica.lag.time.max.ms because of broker-3's 9 s GC and broker-2's slow disk; (b) network partition (ruled out by metrics); (c) a mass leader election. (a) fits.
  4. How I'd verify: kafka-topics.sh --describe --under-replicated-partitions; broker GC logs; iostat -x; fetch-lag per replica.
  5. Root cause: Two followers dropped out of the ISR for different reasons, leaving the leader alone; broker correctly refuses acks=all writes since 2 copies cannot be guaranteed. The system chose consistency over availability, as designed.
  6. Fix: Short term: recover followers, let ISR re-expand; then review heap and disk. Long term: right-size heap/G1 settings, separate disks, add brokers.
  7. Prevention: Alerts on ISR shrink rate, disk await, GC pauses; capacity headroom; chaos test a broker loss.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Lowering min.insync to 1 would restore writes but any leader failure would then lose acknowledged payments; one-way damage. I would also not enable unclean election.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Business insists on availability for a non-money topic? -> Per-topic min.insync=1 is a legitimate, documented decision.
  • Leader dies while ISR is {leader} only? -> Partition offline until a ISR member returns (unclean off).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a "quick" min.insync=1 change during an incident was never reverted; a later broker crash lost a few hundred acknowledged transactions.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: lowers min.insync.
  • Hire: explains the CP choice and fixes followers.
  • Strong hire: adds decision gravity, leader shifting, alerts and per-topic policy.

questions.promptHtml: How do you choose the number of partitions for a topic, and what happens if you need to change it later?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is a one-way-door decision that affects ordering, parallelism and operations.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I derive it from the target throughput divided by what one consumer handles, then add headroom, rather than from broker count. Partitions can be increased but never decreased, and increasing changes the key-to-partition mapping so ordering per key is broken across the change. I start moderately (say 12 or 24) and grow deliberately.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Partitions are the unit of parallelism: a group cannot have more active consumers than partitions. Per-partition write throughput is roughly 5-10 MB/s (benchmark), so consumer speed usually drives the count. Costs of too many: more file handles, longer leader election and recovery, longer rebalances, more replication overhead. Records with the same key go to hash(key) % partitions; adding partitions remaps keys, so a key's older messages sit in one partition and newer in another, breaking per-key order during transition.

parts = max(target MB/s / per-partition MB/s, target msg/s / per-consumer msg/s) x headroom

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Sizing by broker count.
  • Adding partitions to a keyed, order-sensitive topic without a drain/migration plan.
  • Assuming partitions can be reduced.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you grow safely for ordered data? -> Create a new topic with more partitions, dual-consume, cut over after draining the old one.
  2. Why are very large partition counts risky? -> Recovery time, controller load, memory/file handles (KRaft eases this; verify limits).
  3. What about hot keys? -> More partitions do not help one hot key; salt or split the key.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "more partitions = more throughput". Senior: derive from consumer capacity, know the ordering break and the cost curve.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team doubled partitions on a keyed order topic and saw "cancel" events processed before "create" for a few minutes.

questions.contextHtml:
Cluster: 6 brokers, 64 GB RAM each (16 GB heap), 50 MB/s ingest. At 10:15 a data-science team starts a backfill reading a topic from 3 days ago at full speed. Immediately, p99 produce latency jumps from 8 ms to 400 ms and real-time consumers show lag rising. Metrics:

broker CPU: 25%      network: 40%
disk read IOPS: 300 -> 9,000 on broker-1,4
page cache hit ratio (node exporter): 98% -> 61%
GC: normal

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add brokers" or "tune GC"; ignores that reads are competing with the cache.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which topic and how many consumers in the backfill? Are replicas and the active segment on the same disks? Quotas configured?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Throttle the backfill group with a consumer quota (consumer_byte_rate), or pause it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) cold reads evicting hot pages and saturating disk; (b) leader imbalance; (c) a noisy network. Cache hit drop and read IOPS point to (a).
  4. How I'd verify: iostat -x, vmstat, per-broker fetch metrics, kafka-consumer-groups for the backfill client id.
  5. Root cause: Kafka relies on the page cache for tail reads and writes. Historical reads fetch cold segments from disk and push out recent pages, so tail consumers and follower fetches now hit disk too, amplifying the slowdown.
  6. Fix: Short term: client quotas. Long term: backfills read from a replica/mirror cluster or from tiered storage/object-store copy (verify availability), separate topic mirror, scheduled off-peak.
  7. Prevention: Quotas by default for batch clients; dashboard for cache hit ratio and disk await.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not raising the broker heap; that steals RAM from the page cache and makes it worse.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did the heap not matter? -> The data path avoids the JVM heap via page cache and sendfile.
  • With SSDs would it vanish? -> It softens, not removes, since cache and IOPS contention remain.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a "harmless" analytics replay at 2 pm doubled checkout event latency until a quota was applied.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames GC/CPU.
  • Hire: identifies cache eviction and throttles.
  • Strong hire: separates workloads structurally and mentions quotas and heap-vs-cache.

questions.contextHtml: A clickstream topic has 1-hour retention to save disk (100 MB/s ingest, RF=3). The downstream consumer is down for a 3-hour outage after a bad release. When it recovers, it logs OffsetOutOfRangeException and, because auto.offset.reset=latest, jumps to the end. Analytics later shows a 2-hour hole. Disk use was 8% so nobody objected to longer retention.
questions.promptHtml: What happened and how should retention and consumer config be set?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the consumer for being down; proposes "just set retention to 30 days".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the recovery-time objective for consumers? Can data be reproduced? What is the cost of disk (100 MB/s x 86,400 = 8.6 TB/day raw x 3)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Backfill the 2 hours from the source (app logs/object store) if it exists; reset offsets deliberately.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Retention shorter than the outage; reset=latest hides the gap silently; size-based retention may also cut earlier.
  4. How I'd verify: Topic configs (kafka-configs.sh --describe); earliest vs committed offsets; consumer logs.
  5. Root cause: Segments were deleted before the consumer read them, so its committed offset no longer existed; latest skipped to the end without an error.
  6. Fix: Retention at least 2-3x the worst realistic outage plus recovery time (for example 24-72 h, costing 8.6 TB/day x RF 3 about 26 TB/day, so budget accordingly or use compression/tiered storage); auto.offset.reset=earliest or none so the gap is an error not silence.
  7. Prevention: Alert on lag in time, with a threshold at 50% of retention; document consumer SLOs.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: 30 days "just in case" costs about 780 TB raw at this rate; I would not guess, I would price it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cheaper way to keep a long history? -> Sink to object storage (Parquet) and keep Kafka short.
  • Does retention.bytes change this? -> Whichever limit hits first deletes data.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: data loss was discovered a week later via a revenue dip; the root cause was a silent latest reset.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raises retention without numbers.
  • Hire: ties retention to outage duration and fixes reset policy.
  • Strong hire: prices options, alerts on lag-time vs retention, uses archival.

questions.contextHtml: Product says: "New services must start with every customer's current profile, and when a customer deletes their account we must stop serving their data." There are 4M customers, about 20 updates each per year, 2 KB per record. The architect proposes a delete-retention topic with 365 days.
questions.promptHtml: What do you ask, and what do you propose?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Accepts the design; ignores deletion and bootstrap time.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the maximum bootstrap time? How soon after deletion must data vanish (legal deadline)? Do consumers cache profiles? Is history needed or only current state?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; this is design.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Delete retention replays 80M records (160 GB) at start; compaction gives about 4M (8 GB) and supports tombstones.
  4. How I'd verify: Prototype and time a bootstrap at 100 MB/s (8 GB about 80 s versus about 27 minutes).
  5. Root cause of the problem with the proposal: A time-retained topic cannot delete one key before the year ends, so it fails the deletion requirement.
  6. Fix: cleanup.policy=compact, key=customer id, tombstone on deletion; tune min.cleanable.dirty.ratio, delete.retention.ms longer than the slowest consumer's catch-up; consumers must handle tombstones by evicting caches.
  7. Prevention: Test with a slow consumer; monitor cleaner lag.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Compaction does not instantly remove data; if the legal deadline is hard, add a purge job or encrypt per-user keys.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need full history for audit? -> Separate delete-retention topic or archive.
  • A consumer is offline longer than delete.retention.ms? -> It may miss the tombstone; resync from scratch.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a deleted user kept receiving emails because a downstream cache never processed the tombstone.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts 365 days.
  • Hire: proposes compaction plus tombstones.
  • Strong hire: asks the legal deadline, bootstrap math and tombstone window.

questions.contextHtml: The keyed orders topic (key=orderId, 12 partitions, 20 MB/s) is saturating its 12 consumers (each at 95% CPU). You must go to 48 partitions with zero downtime. Order events for the same order must stay in order (CREATED, PAID, SHIPPED). Peak traffic is in 3 hours.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: kafka-topics.sh --alter --partitions 48 and done.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How long does an order live (minutes or days)? Is the consumer idempotent? Can I stop producers briefly? Is a relaxed order tolerable for old orders?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Short term, make consumers cheaper (batch DB writes) to buy headroom before the peak.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Simple alter remaps hash(key) % 48, so in-flight orders hop partitions and events may be processed out of order by different consumers.
  4. How I'd verify: Replay a sample of keys on a staging copy and measure reordered keys.
  5. Root cause of risk: The partition mapping depends on partition count.
  6. Fix: Create orders.v2 with 48 partitions; producers dual-write (or a mirror job copies) to both; start v2 consumers in parallel with idempotent handlers; drain v1 (lag 0, all in-flight orders finished); switch consumers to v2 only and then producers; retire v1. Alternatively, if orders are short-lived, alter partitions during a quiet window and accept a brief overlap.
  7. Prevention: Choose headroom initially; consumer parallelism SLO monitoring.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not do this right before peak, nor skip the idempotency, since dual-consumption duplicates.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cheaper alternative? -> Make each consumer faster with internal worker threads keyed by order id.
  • Rollback? -> Keep v1 live until v2 is verified.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: an in-place alter broke ordering for a few thousand orders; "shipped" processed before "paid" created manual refunds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: simple alter.
  • Hire: new-topic cutover with drain.
  • Strong hire: addresses ordering, dedup, timing and rollback; considers consumer-side optimization first.
